text: Let's talk about fear, because I think a lot of people are scared to raise their prices. Oh, I was terrified. The first time I raised my price from $9 to $49, I thought everyone would leave. And did they? Sales went up, not down, up. When it was cheap, people didn't trust it. When it was forty-nine dollars, they assumed it worked. That is wild. Cheaper made it look worse. Cheap tells people you don't believe in it either. Price is a message, not just a number.
first_line: Let's talk about fear, because I think a lot of people are scared to raise their prices.
last_line: Price is a message, not just a number.

text: A chain opened across the street and sold croissants for a dollar. Mine were four. In six weeks my revenue dropped by 70%. 70%? That's brutal. It was terrifying. I remember sitting in the walk-in fridge, crying, because it was the only place nobody could hear me. And here's the part nobody tells you. The business didn't fail because of the chain. It failed because I never knew my numbers.

last_line: It failed because I never knew my numbers.

text: If someone is watching this and their business is struggling right now, what should they do tonight? Write down what one sale actually costs you. Not what you think, what it actually costs. If you can't answer that in one minute, stop spending money until you can. Because you can survive a bad month. You cannot survive not knowing why it was bad.

last_line: You cannot survive not knowing why it was bad.

text: So how do you go from that bedroom to where you are now? I started teaching other bakers how to price. One spreadsheet. I sold it for nine dollars on a Tuesday night and by Friday I had made eleven thousand dollars. 11,000 dollars from a spreadsheet. From a spreadsheet. That's when I realized the thing that broke me was the thing other people needed most.

text: What's the biggest lie people believe about starting a business? That you need a great idea. You don't. My idea was a spreadsheet. You need a painful problem and the guts to charge for fixing it. Last question. Would you open the bakery again? Honestly, yes. But this time I would know my numbers on day one, and I would put the stars in the shop.

text: What do you mean you didn't know your numbers? I didn't know that every croissant cost me two dollars and ten cents to make. I was proud of my margins and I didn't even have margins. That's honestly the most common mistake I hear on this show. It is. Most people think they have a sales problem. Ninety per cent of the time they have a pricing problem.

text: Okay, so you close the bakery, then what? Then I moved back in with my parents. Twenty seven years old, sleeping in my childhood bedroom, with glow in the dark stars on the ceiling. No way, the stars were still up. The stars were still up. My mom refused to take them down. She said I would need them again some day. She was right, by the way.
